title: Rebuilding Incumbents for AI Beats Investing in Startups
dek: AI's impact on the economy is uneven: restaurants and golf courses are untouched, but incumbents with brands, licenses and network effects can become market leaders once they are engineered.
why: Medium information density, but it offers a counterintuitive investment framework: don't fund startups, buy incumbents and rebuild the organization with an engineering team. For anyone watching AI deployment and M&A.
who: Investors and founders focused on AI deployment, M&A and incumbent transformation, especially those who want to understand the logic of "don't back startups, buy the leader."
skip: The founder-reflection segment from 34:45 to 36:08, which is low density.

points.h: AI's impact on the economy is uneven
points.body: Michael Lee argues AI will not change every industry evenly. Restaurants and golf courses are industries AI will never touch; in coding, startups will win — he notes that Conviction and Sequence were about to buy an outsourced coding shop, which sounds like a terrible idea, but you would put your money into Cognition or Anthropic. What actually excites him is the third category: incumbents with brands, scale, network effects or regulatory moats. If you can graft the most advanced technology and engineering onto them, you have a shot at turning them into market leaders. Sequence's entire model rests on this judgment.

Michael uses "every company has a celebrity" to explain why incumbents cannot complete the AI transition on their own. At Blackstone the celebrity is the investor, which is how it unites the world's largest capital allocators; but in a world that believes alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need the engineer to be the celebrity who commands respect. Palantir is essentially a collection of world-class engineers wrapped in a shell and sold to organizations that cannot hire such people. If you cannot hire them yourself, going to service providers like Accenture or McKinsey does not work either — their incentive is to keep you paying, and their path is incrementalism. Buying software is worse: software sells the workflows that already exist today, while AI requires redesigning a human assembly line that does not yet exist.

points.h: Banks are the perfect cold-start testbed
points.body: When Sequence was founded it faced a cold-start problem: no money means no deals, no deals means no engineers, no engineers means nobody gives you money. They decided to land a customer first to prove themselves. Through a friend's introduction they reached a family bank in Georgia, entered as a service provider last August, and worked on key workflows for several months. The bank then asked whether they wanted to become a permanent partner, which became Sequence's first investment, closing in March this year, with approvals from the Fed and the OCC along the way. Michael says banks being regulated is a feature, not a bug: operations are clearly defined, data hygiene is excellent, and it is a great fit for agents.

points.h: Insurance brokerage is the archetypal incumbent
points.body: Sequence spent a lot of time studying insurance brokerage. More than $2 trillion in premiums flows to insurers each year, brokers do not charge clients — insurers pay them — customer retention runs as high as 90%, and brokers can hardly compete on price; these traits make it extremely hard for startups to break in. Michael says insurers' underwriting business has barely been profitable through history, with profits coming mainly from investments, which gives them an incentive to accumulate assets, and that in turn makes brokers very powerful. Baldwin meets all of Sequence's criteria: a huge market, an incumbent insulated from startup risk, and a management team already pushing technology deployment.

points.h: Atlas abstracts 80% of the commonality for reuse
points.body: Atlas is the platform Sequence built inside the bank, and they expect it to generalize across every industry. That judgment comes from an observation: if you break a business into atomic units, 80% is highly homogeneous and 20% is vertical-specific. Atlas has four layers: the first is the data ontology, defining in code how the organization and business run so models can understand the company; the second is the agent builder, building high-performance agents on top of that data; the third is called lattice, the orchestration mechanism that actually wires agents into workflows; and on top is artifacts, the application-building layer. Michael says all the core infrastructure they built in the bank can be reused for Baldwin and any future company.

Michael concedes large PE firms have the incentive, resources and capability to do AI transformation, but he thinks they face several structural constraints. The first is talent: a typical PE firm is designed to make the investor the celebrity, while world-class engineers want to be in the decision-making; a 25-year-old engineer having a say in investment decisions at a large buyout firm is very rare. The second is time horizon: under a fund structure you are usually thinking about how to package and sell in three years, a completely different formula from the long-term commitment technology transformation requires. The third is deal cadence: Sequence does one deal a year, with no deployment cadence and no LP pushing them to invest more this year. Michael says he wants to hold Sequence equity for life.

points.h: The hard numbers from the bank rebuild
points.body: From the March investment to the recording, about 6 months, Sequence built a system in the bank that can take on all consumer lending in the organization. Average consumer loan underwriting volume fell 94% versus March. Commercial loan underwriting began rolling out in recent months, and average loan processing time dropped from 30 days to 11 days. Michael says this lets the bank take on far more loan volume with the same headcount. In this year's second quarter, the bank's loan volume doubled versus the first quarter. Historically the bank had turned customers away because of limited middle- and back-office bandwidth; now, with underwriting standards completely unchanged, the bank handled all the loan volume, and with a smaller underwriting team than before the investment — because one person retired and one moved to the front office.

points.h: Betting on people beats betting on ideas
points.body: Michael says if he were redesigning how to do PE today, he would only look for exceptional people solving complex problems in huge markets. From his experience at Sequence he learned that ideas are cheap, execution is very hard, and truly exceptional people always find a way to make things happen — because they bring in people who cover their weaknesses, or they are persistent enough to find backers to do what everyone thinks is crazy. He says everything else, whether it is the best idea you have ever seen or the hottest breakthrough of the moment, is only an important signal, but this business today ultimately comes down to people, especially at the early stage.
